pieces.h: Exam Details
pieces.t: Georgia does not operate one single statewide journeyman electrician exam for every individual electrician. State-level electrical contractor licensing is administered through the Georgia State Board of Electrical Contractors, while journeyman-level requirements may be tied to local jurisdictions, apprenticeship completion, employer standards, or a recognized trades examination. A commonly used journeyman-level electrical exam format is the ICC National Standard Journeyman Electrician exam. The ICC National Standard Journeyman Electrician exam includes 80 multiple-choice questions, allows 4 hours of testing time, and is open book. Its content areas include general knowledge, services and service equipment, feeders, branch circuits and conductors, wiring methods and materials, equipment and devices, control devices, motors and generators, and special occupancies, equipment, and conditions.

pieces.h: Open Book Test
pieces.t: The ICC National Standard Journeyman Electrician exam is an open book test. Candidates taking that exam may use approved reference materials during testing, subject to the exam provider’s rules. Open book testing requires strong code-navigation skills because candidates must find information quickly, understand the code language, and apply it correctly under timed conditions. Open book does not mean the exam is simple. The National Electrical Code is a detailed technical reference, and a candidate who is unfamiliar with its structure can lose valuable time searching through unrelated sections. The included National Electrical Code 2026 Paperback with Tabs helps candidates practice using the NEC before exam day, so article locations, chapter organization, tables, definitions, and major subject areas become more familiar. Candidates should work through questions by identifying the subject first, selecting the most likely NEC article or table, confirming the correct rule, and answering carefully.

pieces.h: Licensing Steps
pieces.t: Georgia electrical licensing depends on the level of credential being pursued. Electrical contractors are licensed at the state level through the Georgia State Board of Electrical Contractors. Journeyman-level recognition may be connected to local requirements, apprenticeship completion, employer standards, or a recognized journeyman-level examination. pieces.h: State Requirements
pieces.t: Georgia licenses electrical contractors through the Georgia State Board of Electrical Contractors. The state electrical contractor license structure includes restricted and non-restricted classifications. A restricted electrical contractor license is limited in scope, while a non-restricted license provides broader electrical contracting authority. Georgia does not issue one uniform statewide individual journeyman electrician license in the same way many other states do. Instead, journeyman-level status may be recognized through local jurisdictions, employer classifications, apprenticeship progression, or exam-based credentialing used by a city, county, or organization. For workers preparing for journeyman-level work, the typical career path includes completing electrical training, gaining supervised field experience, learning the National Electrical Code, building electrical calculation skills, and demonstrating practical competence. pieces.h: Exam Details
pieces.t: Georgia electrical contractor licensing is handled by the Georgia Construction Industry Licensing Board, Division of Electrical Contractors, under the Georgia Secretary of State. The Board reviews applications and determines whether an applicant is approved to sit for the examination. The examination is administered through PSI as a computer-based test at PSI test centers. Georgia offers electrical contractor examinations for Class I Restricted and Class II Non-Restricted licenses. Both examinations are multiple-choice exams and are administered in two parts. The candidate handbook states that eight hours are allotted to complete both parts of the exam, with four hours for Part I followed by a break, and four hours for Part II. The time limit includes beta questions. The Georgia electrical contractor examination content is divided into Regulations, Laws, and Administrative Functions and Technical Functions. Regulations, Laws, and Administrative Functions include compliance with laws, regulations, administrative requirements, and work planning.

pieces.h: Exam Details
pieces.t: Technical Functions include electrical circuits, electrical controls and devices, rotating equipment, lighting systems, raceway systems, wiring systems, grounding systems, special systems, service equipment, and additional trade functions listed in the exam outline. The Class I and Class II exams both include 30 questions in Regulations, Laws, and Administrative Functions and 110 questions in Technical Functions. The candidate handbook also identifies beta questions that are included in the total number of examination questions. The Class I exam includes 15 beta questions, and the Class II exam includes 22 beta questions. Beta questions are used for exam development and do not count toward the final score. The minimum passing final scaled score for each Georgia electrical contractor examination is 70. After the examination, PSI provides the candidate with a score report. PSI also provides the official score report to the Board, and Board staff communicates with the applicant regarding results and next steps.

pieces.t: Tabs help candidates become more familiar with NEC organization during preparation, including article locations, definitions, wiring methods, conductor rules, service requirements, grounding and bonding, overcurrent protection, motors, equipment, and special systems. For open-book preparation, candidates should practice with their references before test day. A strong routine includes using the table of contents, index, article structure, tables, notes, exceptions, and cross-references. Candidates should also practice answering exam-style questions without immediately looking up every answer. The goal is to build enough knowledge to recognize the subject area quickly and then confirm the answer efficiently with the correct reference.

pieces.h: Licensing Steps
pieces.t: Georgia electrical contractor candidates begin by choosing the correct license classification. The Class I Restricted license and the Class II Non-Restricted license have different scopes and experience expectations. Candidates pursuing broad electrical contractor authority usually focus on the Class II Non-Restricted path. The applicant must submit the required application to the Georgia Construction Industry Licensing Board, Division of Electrical Contractors. The Board must approve the applicant before the applicant can sit for the exam. The application requires documentation and information related to the license type selected. Experience must be gained under a licensed electrical contractor and documented through the required forms. For the Class I Restricted license, the applicant must document experience in at least six of the primary experience areas.

pieces.h: Licensing Steps
pieces.t: For the Class II Non-Restricted license, the applicant must document experience in all primary experience areas and experience with electrical installations in excess of single-phase, 400-ampere systems while working under a Class II Non-Restricted licensed contractor. The experience record must show at least four years of qualifying experience gained under a licensed contractor. After the Board approves the application, the applicant receives approval to sit for the exam. PSI provides the candidate information needed to register and schedule the examination. Candidates are responsible for scheduling the exam by the posted deadline, following PSI’s test-day instructions, bringing required identification, and using only approved materials during the exam. After the exam is completed, PSI provides results to the candidate and to the Board. Passing the examination is one part of the licensure process. The Board completes the licensing process after receiving official results and confirming that the applicant has satisfied the requirements for the license classification.

pieces.h: State Requirements
pieces.t: Georgia regulates electrical contractors through the Georgia Construction Industry Licensing Board, Division of Electrical Contractors. Electrical contractors are licensed at the state level, and applicants must meet the Board’s requirements before receiving a license. The Board offers Class I Restricted and Class II Non-Restricted electrical contractor licenses. The Class I Restricted license is limited compared with the Class II license. The Class II Non-Restricted license is the broader classification and is associated with unrestricted electrical contractor work within the state licensing structure. Candidates should select the license classification that matches the work they intend to perform and the experience they can document. Georgia’s application process requires candidates to file through the Secretary of State licensing system and provide the required documentation. Applications are reviewed by the Board. Completed applications may be reviewed by Board staff and may be presented to the Board at a scheduled meeting. Incomplete applications may delay approval.

pieces.h: Test Information and Study Materials
pieces.t: This Ultimate Combo gives Georgia candidates several ways to prepare. The Georgia Master Electrician Study Guide supports broad review of electrical contractor exam content. The Electrician Calculations Study Guide gives candidates dedicated practice with math and formula work. The National Electrical Code 2026 Paperback with Tabs helps candidates build code familiarity and reference-navigation habits. Candidates preparing for the Georgia electrical contractor exam should study both administrative and technical topics. Administrative preparation should include laws, workers’ compensation, unemployment insurance, tax responsibilities, Board requirements, permits, inspections, insurance, bonding, bookkeeping, contracts, bidding, scheduling, and project management.

pieces.h: Test Information and Study Materials
pieces.t: Technical preparation should include circuits, controls, motors, lighting, raceways, wiring systems, grounding, special systems, service equipment, equipment installation, troubleshooting, and code-based installation rules. Calculations should be practiced throughout the study process. Electrical calculation questions require candidates to identify the correct method, select the correct formula or table, use the proper units, and check the answer for reasonableness. Repeated calculation practice helps candidates reduce errors and become more comfortable solving problems during long testing sessions. Code navigation should also be part of regular study. Candidates should practice using the NEC table of contents, index, definitions, article structure, tables, notes, exceptions, and cross-references. During an open-book exam, a candidate who knows where to look has a major advantage over a candidate who is searching randomly. Flash cards are useful for shorter review sessions and repeated reinforcement.
